title: Demonstrationes circa residua ex divisione potestatum per numeros primos resultantia

deep.reconstruction:
This page finishes Theorem 76 and draws consequences for the quadratic character of +3 and -3.

**End of the proof of Theorem 76.** Let P = 3n-1 be prime. Then gcd(3, P-1) = 1, so cubing x -> x^3 is a bijection on (Z/P)^*. Hence the cubes of 1, ..., P-1 leave pairwise distinct residues. So P never divides g^3 - f^3 with f ≢ g (mod P) and f, g ≢ 0. Since g^3 - f^3 = (g-f)(f^2+fg+g^2), P never divides f^2+fg+g^2 with f, g not divisible by P. The case f ≡ g gives 3f^2, which P (≠ 3) does not divide either. The previous page reduced f^2+fg+g^2 to the form p^2+3q^2. Conversely, p^2+3q^2 = f^2+fg+g^2 with f = p-q, g = 2q. So no p^2+3q^2 (with p, q prime to P) is divisible by such a P. The statement extends to every number of the form 3n-1, since each has at least one prime factor of that form.

Combined with the previous page this gives the theorem: an odd prime P ≠ 3 divides some p^2+3q^2 with P not dividing q if and only if P ≡ 1 (mod 3). For P ≡ 1 (mod 3) this used three distinct cube roots of a common residue, i.e. nontrivial cube roots of unity.

**Corollary 1 (§77).** If P = 3n+1 divides p^2+3q^2 and q^2 ≡ γ, then p^2 ≡ -3γ. Hence -3 (equivalently 3n-2 mod P) is a quadratic residue mod P.

**Corollary 2 (§78).** For P = 3n-1, -3 (equivalently 3n-4) is a non-residue.

In modern terms: (-3/P) = 1 if and only if P ≡ 1 (mod 3).

**Scholion (§79), worked out on the next page.** Every prime > 3 is ≡ 1, 5, 7 or 11 (mod 12). Combining with (-1/P) = 1 iff P ≡ 1 (mod 4), and multiplicativity of the Legendre symbol, Euler gets:
- P ≡ 1 (mod 12): both +3 and -3 are residues.
- P ≡ 5: neither is.
- P ≡ 7: only -3 is.
- P ≡ 11: only +3 is.

This is the supplementary case of quadratic reciprocity for 3. The purpose of the paper is to derive residue theorems from power residues; Euler himself remarks on the next page that the cubic route is 'satis obliqua' and wants a more natural proof.
errors: Minor gap: the statements implicitly require that P does not divide q (or p), i.e. f, g not divisible by the prime. Trivially P | p^2+3q^2 when P | p and P | q. Euler leaves this tacit.
The case f ≡ g (mod P) is not discussed explicitly. It is harmless because 3f^2 is not divisible by P ≠ 3.
The extension to composite 3n-1 is correct as stated: such a number always has a prime factor ≡ 2 (mod 3).

ideas.what: For primes P ≡ 2 (mod 3), cubing permutes the nonzero residues, so P never divides f^2+fg+g^2 or p^2+3q^2 except trivially.
ideas.modern_name: x -> x^3 is an automorphism of (Z/P)^* when gcd(3, P-1) = 1; primes inert in Z[ω]

ideas.what: -3 is a quadratic residue mod P if and only if P ≡ 1 (mod 3), proved via cubic residues.
ideas.modern_name: Quadratic character of -3 (supplement to quadratic reciprocity)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (conjectured in the 1740s); proofs by Euler and by Lagrange (1775); treated by Gauss, Disquisitiones Arithmeticae §§117-120
ideas.where_published: E449 (Opuscula analytica I); earlier related results in E272

ideas.what: Classification of the residuosity of +3 and -3 by P mod 12.

deep.surprise_reason: This is Euler's known proof of the quadratic character of ±3 via cubic residues in E449. It is cited in standard histories and by Gauss. The page offers nothing new to the record.
